newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Bank of Israel maintains tight monetary policy.
newsitem.headline: Bank of Israel maintains tight monetary policy.

text.p: The Bank of Israel disappointed financial markets on Monday, announcing it would not lower interest rates in December.
But economists were not surprised, saying they expected real rates to remain high over the next few months.
After the Tel Aviv stock market closed, the Bank of Israel said its key lending rate in December would remain at the present level of an annualised 15.2 percent.
"The decision is expected to have a negative impact on (stock) trading as investors were waiting for a cut of 0.2 to 0.3 percentage point," Amitay Tafla of Sigma Securities said.
"In the forex trading we saw an immediate reaction and the shekel started rising against the dollar. The Israeli shares traded on Nasdaq were also falling following the announcement."
As long as the 1997 budget is still being formulated "the Bank of Israel is certainly not hurrying to bring down the interest rate sharply," said Ptachia Bar-Shavit, chief economist at Bank Hapoalim.
The central bank, concerned with inflation, says it cannot ease up on monetary policy until the government makes a substantial effort to tighten fiscal policy.
Last week, the government announced plans for an additional cut of two billion shekels from next year's 190.8 billion shekel spending package.

Legislators, meanwhile, are still haggling over the government's original budget proposal, which included a hefty 4.9 billion shekel cut. The cuts have drawn strong opposition even from the Likud-led government's coalition partners, who say low-income families will be hit the hardest.
Parliament has until December 31 to pass the 1997 budget.
Without full support from its own coalition partners, the government will have a hard time getting its budget approved.

This could force Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to step back from his campaign promise not to raise taxes, said Yoram Gabbay, head of the portfolio management company Peilim and former director of the state revenue administration.
"In the end, I believe the government will balance out budget cuts with tax hikes," Gabbay said.
He said the government will likely raise taxes that do not need parliamentary approval -- such as levies on fuel and cigarettes and value added taxes.

The business sector has slammed the central bank's monetary policy, saying it artifically strengthened the shekel and hurt exports. Industrialists say high interest rates are slowing growth at a time when the economy is already weakening.
But this argument is unlikely to sway the central bank.
"The experience in the western world is that even in a recession, if there is big budget deficit central banks keep interest rates high," Gabbay said.

In fact, because market expectations for inflation in the next 12 months are falling, real interest rates will rise, economists noted. With inflation over the next 12 months expected to be only nine percent or even less, real interest rates now stand at about six percent.
The Israeli shekel, therefore, is not likely to depreciate.

"The creation of a balance (in the foreign exchange market) requires a sharp decline in the Bank of Israel's monetary tender rate, which it is very hard to think will happpen in the near future," Bar-Shavit said.
($1 = 3.25 shekels)
